messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet Nguyen is an eighteen-year-old Vietnamese-American photographer who presents with a PCL-5 score of 77, referred for psychological assessment following a period of escalating behavioural dysregulation. He is single, lives alone in a studio apartment, and has been working freelance since leaving military service several months ago — an exit that was not planned so much as forced by the events described below.

Kiet enlisted at seventeen with a waiver, drawn by a combination of economic pressure and what he describes as a genuine desire to do something that mattered. He was deployed as part of a small forward unit, and it was during a patrol through a village compound that the defining event occurred. His unit came under ambush. In the chaos, a younger soldier — barely older than Kiet himself — was struck and went down in a narrow alley. Kiet had been positioned closest to him. He froze for what he estimates was no more than seconds, but in that interval the soldier died. The sounds were specific: the crack of incoming fire, then a wet, collapsing silence. He has not been able to hear a car backfire, a door slamming in a corridor, or the sharp pop of a camera flash unit misfiring without his body responding as though the ambush is still happening. In his current work as a photographer — shooting events, street scenes, the occasional editorial assignment — these sounds are not rare. A burst shutter, a lighting rig falling, the percussion of a crowd: any of these can instantly return him to that alley without transition or warning, the memory arriving not as recollection but as re-immersion, more textured and immediate than anything in his waking life.

When those memories surface, what follows is not grief but rage — a rage he finds frightening in its intensity, directed sometimes outward, sometimes inward. The rage feeds directly back into how he understands what happened: he had been closest, he had the training, and he had failed. He has come to believe, with a certainty that resists any counter-argument, that he should have protected the other soldier and did not. This conviction — that he is someone who fails when it counts — has metastasised into a broader sense that he belongs nowhere, that the person who came home is not someone any community would recognise or want. He mistrusts the motives of almost everyone he encounters, reading ordinary professional interactions as performances concealing judgment or contempt. These appraisals of himself and the world keep the threat system perpetually engaged: Kiet cannot relax even in environments he knows to be objectively safe. He sits with his back to walls in cafés, scans rooftops from habit when he is on location, and describes his body as never fully standing down.

That chronic state of hyperarousal, in turn, makes him acutely sensitive to the sensory environment — which means the triggers find him more readily, and the memories break through more often. Each intrusion renews the evidence, in his own mind, that he is damaged and culpable: the very fact that he cannot control the memories confirms, to him, that something is fundamentally wrong with who he is. The loop has become self-sustaining. His mistrust of others has meant he has turned down collaborative photographic work, preferring solitary assignments where he can control his environment — but the isolation reinforces the belief that he belongs nowhere, and the solitary work still places him in unpredictable urban settings where triggering sounds are unavoidable.

There is one further dimension worth noting in isolation: Kiet has been taking risks that have alarmed the few people who remain in contact with him — driving at speed without apparent purpose, accepting assignments in genuinely dangerous locations without adequate preparation. He does not fully explain this behaviour, but does not deny it either.

What finally brought him to seek help was a photographic assignment at a street festival where a series of fireworks were set off without warning. He left the scene, sat in his car for two hours, and, by his own account, could not account for approximately forty minutes of that time. He is most afraid that what happened in that alley has made him into something irreparable. He is most hoping, though he states this with visible difficulty, that someone might be able to tell him otherwise.
